points.title: The role of consumers
points.brief: A consumer buys and uses goods and services to meet needs and wants, and consumers' spending decides what businesses make.

points.title: What influences consumer decisions
points.brief: Price, income, quality, advertising, friends and family, social media and ethical concerns all shape what consumers buy.

points.title: Pros and cons of payment methods
points.brief: Debit spends your own money, credit and buy now pay later borrow it and can add interest and late fees, and cash is easy to track but easy to lose.

points.title: Scams and identity theft
points.brief: Scams trick people out of money or details, and identity theft uses stolen personal details. Consumers guard against them by checking sellers and never sharing passwords.

points.title: Consumer guarantees
points.brief: Under the Australian Consumer Law, goods must be of acceptable quality, fit for purpose and match their description, whatever the store's own policy says.

points.title: Refunds, repairs and replacements
points.brief: A major fault gives the consumer a choice of refund or replacement, and a minor fault lets the business choose to repair it first.

points.title: Organisations that help consumers
points.brief: The ACCC, NSW Fair Trading and ombudsman services handle complaints, enforce consumer laws and warn people about scams.

points.title: Borrowing money
points.brief: People borrow through personal loans, credit cards and home loans, and repay it with interest. The interest rate, fees and term decide what a loan really costs.

points.title: Budgeting
points.brief: A budget lists income and expenses so spending stays within income and money is set aside for savings goals.

points.title: Superannuation
points.brief: Superannuation is money saved for retirement, paid by employers into a super fund as a share of an employee's wages.

points.title: Help with financial difficulty
points.brief: People in money trouble can ask their lender for a hardship arrangement, see a free financial counsellor, or as a last resort go bankrupt.

points.title: The economic problem of scarcity
points.brief: Resources are limited but people's wants are unlimited, so every society must choose what to produce, how and for whom.

points.title: Opportunity cost
points.brief: Opportunity cost is the next best thing given up when making a choice, such as the wage lost by studying instead of working.

points.title: The circular flow of income
points.brief: Households sell their labour to businesses for income, and spend it on goods and services, so money flows around the economy.

points.title: The price mechanism
points.brief: In a market, buyers' demand and sellers' supply meet to set a price. A shortage pushes the price up and a surplus pushes it down.

points.title: Economic growth
points.brief: Economic growth is an increase in the goods and services an economy produces over time, measured by the change in gross domestic product (GDP).

points.title: Effects of economic growth in Australia
points.brief: Growth brings more jobs, higher incomes and more tax for services, but can also bring inflation, inequality and harm to the environment.

points.title: Government economic objectives
points.brief: Governments aim for steady growth, low unemployment, low and stable inflation and a fair share of income.

points.title: Why governments intervene
points.brief: Governments step into the economy to provide public goods, protect consumers and the environment, reduce inequality and smooth out booms and slumps.

points.title: How governments intervene
points.brief: Governments act through taxes and spending in the budget, laws and regulation, and payments such as welfare, while the Reserve Bank sets interest rates.

points.title: The goals of a business
points.brief: Businesses aim for profit, growth, market share, good service and sometimes social or environmental goals.

points.title: Types of businesses
points.brief: Businesses can be sole traders, partnerships or companies, and small, medium or large, each with its own features.

points.title: Inputs, processes and outputs
points.brief: A business turns inputs such as materials, labour and money through processes into outputs, the goods and services it sells.

points.title: Recruiting skilled staff
points.brief: A business finds and chooses staff through job ads, applications, interviews and reference checks, and skilled staff lift its performance.

points.title: The business cycle
points.brief: The economy moves through booms, when sales and jobs grow, and recessions, when they fall, and businesses must adjust to both.

points.title: Ethical business decisions
points.brief: Ethical businesses treat workers, customers and the environment fairly, and corporate social responsibility goes beyond what the law requires.

points.title: What makes an entrepreneur
points.brief: Entrepreneurs spot opportunities, take risks, solve problems and keep going after failures to build something new.

points.title: Entrepreneurs' contribution to society
points.brief: Entrepreneurs create jobs, products and new ways of working, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander entrepreneurs who build businesses on culture and community.

points.title: The rule of law
points.brief: The rule of law means everyone, including the government, must obey the law, and laws are known, fair and applied equally.

points.title: Criminal and civil law
points.brief: Criminal law deals with offences against society, prosecuted by the state. Civil law settles disputes between people, such as over contracts.

points.title: Statute law and common law
points.brief: Statute law is made by parliament. Common law is made by judges when their decisions in cases set precedents for later cases.

points.title: Aboriginal customary lore
points.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities have their own lore, passed down over thousands of years, which guides behaviour and relationships with Country.

points.title: The court hierarchy
points.brief: In NSW, cases start in the Local, District or Supreme Court by seriousness, federal matters go to federal courts, and the High Court is the highest court.

points.title: The Australian Constitution
points.brief: The Constitution sets up the federal parliament, government and High Court, and divides powers between the Commonwealth and the states.

points.title: Three levels of government
points.brief: Federal government handles matters such as defence, state government handles schools and police, and local councils handle rubbish and parks.

points.title: The two houses of federal parliament
points.brief: The House of Representatives forms the government and starts most laws, and the Senate reviews them and represents the states.

points.title: The separation of powers
points.brief: Power is split between parliament, which makes laws, the executive, which carries them out, and the courts, which apply them, so no one group holds all of it.

points.title: Enrolling and voting
points.brief: Australian citizens must enrol at 18 and vote in federal and state elections, and can enrol at 16 so they are ready.

points.title: Voting methods
points.brief: First-past-the-post elects the top vote-getter, preferential voting ranks candidates, and proportional voting gives seats by share of the vote, as in the Senate.

points.title: Compulsory voting
points.brief: Australia makes voting compulsory, which brings high turnout, though some argue people should be free to choose not to vote.

points.title: Parties, independents and forming government
points.brief: A party or coalition with a majority in the House of Representatives forms government. In a hung parliament, a minority government needs independents' support.

points.title: Referendums
points.brief: Changing the Constitution needs a referendum passed by a double majority, a national majority and a majority in at least four states.

points.title: Types of work
points.brief: Work can be paid or unpaid, such as volunteering, and full-time, part-time or casual, as an employee or self-employed.

points.title: Unions and employer groups
points.brief: Trade unions represent workers in dealing with employers, and employer associations represent businesses.

points.title: The changing nature of work
points.brief: Automation, artificial intelligence, working from home and gig work such as food delivery are changing jobs and the skills they need.

points.title: Employers' rights and responsibilities
points.brief: Employers must pay correct wages, keep the workplace safe and treat staff fairly, and can expect staff to work properly and follow reasonable instructions.

points.title: Employees' rights and responsibilities
points.brief: Employees have the right to safety and to be free of discrimination and harassment, and must work safely and follow lawful instructions.

points.title: Awards, agreements and contracts
points.brief: An award sets minimum pay and conditions for an industry, an enterprise agreement is negotiated for one workplace, and a common law contract is made with one worker.

points.title: Resolving workplace disputes
points.brief: Disputes go from a grievance procedure and negotiation to mediation, where a third party helps, and arbitration, where the Fair Work Commission decides.

points.title: How people are paid
points.brief: People are paid wages by the hour, a salary by the year, commission on sales or piece rates per item made.

points.title: Reading a payslip
points.brief: A payslip shows hours, pay rate, gross pay, tax taken out, super paid and net pay, and an income statement totals the year.

points.title: Why we pay tax
points.brief: Taxes pay for public services such as schools, hospitals, roads and welfare, and income tax rises with income.

points.title: Tax file numbers and tax returns
points.brief: Workers need a tax file number so the right tax is taken, and each year they lodge a tax return with the ATO to settle what they owe.

points.title: Children's rights
points.brief: The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, which Australia signed, protects children's rights to safety, education, health and a say.

points.title: Legal capacity and age
points.brief: Legal capacity is the ability to have legal rights and duties, and the law grants them by age, such as working, driving and voting.

points.title: Young people and the police
points.brief: Young people stopped by police have rights, such as to know why and to have an adult present when questioned, and may have to give their name and address.

points.title: Elements of a crime
points.brief: To convict someone, the prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt both the guilty act and the guilty mind.

points.title: Punishments
points.brief: Punishments such as fines, community service and prison aim to deter, protect society, rehabilitate and show the community's disapproval.

points.title: Alternative dispute resolution
points.brief: Mediation, conciliation and arbitration settle disputes outside court, often faster, cheaper and less stressful.

points.title: Circle sentencing
points.brief: Circle sentencing has Aboriginal Elders and community members help a magistrate decide the sentence for an Aboriginal offender.

points.title: Types of investments
points.brief: Common investments are bank deposits, shares, property, bonds, managed funds and superannuation.

points.title: Risk and return
points.brief: Investments that may earn more, such as shares, usually carry more risk of losing money than safer ones, such as term deposits.

points.title: Diversification
points.brief: Spreading money across different investments reduces risk, because a loss on one may be balanced by gains on others.

points.title: Ethical investing
points.brief: Ethical investors avoid companies that harm people or the environment, such as tobacco or coal, and choose ones that do good.

points.title: Protecting investors
points.brief: ASIC regulates financial advisers and markets, and advisers must be licensed and act in their clients' best interests.

points.title: Why businesses promote
points.brief: Businesses promote their goods and services to inform customers, persuade them to buy and remind them the brand exists.

points.title: Target markets and differentiation
points.brief: A target market is the group a product is aimed at, and a business makes its product stand out by price, quality, design or brand.

points.title: Promotion techniques
points.brief: Businesses promote through advertising, social media and influencers, sales promotions such as discounts, personal selling and publicity.

points.title: Misleading advertising
points.brief: The Australian Consumer Law bans false or misleading claims, bait advertising and hidden conditions in ads.

points.title: Advertising to children
points.brief: Ad Standards codes limit advertising to children, such as junk food ads, and require ads to be clearly marked as ads.
